newsitem.title: FRANCE: Russia no threat to NATO, needs partnership - Lebed.
newsitem.headline: Russia no threat to NATO, needs partnership - Lebed.

text.p: Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed said on Thursday that Moscow was no threat to NATO and should seek a new partnership with an enlarged Atlantic alliance.

Lebed, Russia's security chief until President Boris Yeltsin sacked him in October, told the French Institute of International Relations during a private visit to Paris that Russia would never be an enemy of the West.
"We have nothing with which to threaten NATO right now. In our links with NATO, we should confirm the principle of non-deployment of nuclear weapons on the territory of the new members," he said.
"We should also reach a new treaty and set up new partnership ties between Russia and NATO. We must limit the damage caused by the adhesion of new members. That is the priority for Russia."

NATO wants closer ties with Russia, which it recognises as an indispensable part of any future European security arrangement, but is reluctant to sign any document that would give Moscow an effective veto over its decision-making.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, now visiting Moscow, is expected to outline several new initiatives, including the offer of a joint NATO-Russia military brigade, mainly to be used in peacekeeping.
But Lebed said: "I do not understand Albright who proposes that Russia should have a right to vote but not a right of veto...I do not understand what this means."
Lebed, who polled strongly in last year's Russian presidential election, cautioned the West earlier this week against antagonising Russia by admitting eastern European countries to NATO.
He said NATO's enlargement could trigger a new arms race and peripheral Russian regions might be tempted to turn towards the United States, China, Germany or Japan.
"France is politically in NATO but it is not integrated in the command structure. We think we could find a special status for Russia in NATO," he said.

Lebed hailed a Franco-German defence document, saying he was highly interested in the efforts of French President Jacques Chirac and of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl "to integrate Russia in the European security structures".

"I very much appreciate the Franco-German concept on defence, according to which defence is a regional issue," he said. "A certain number of countries would like access to nuclear weapons for example."
